texto:
Local Services Ads (LSA) are a Google advertising format in which local service providers - plumbers, electricians, locksmiths, lawyers, cleaners, estate agents and dozens of other trades - pay for a lead, such as a phone call, message or booking, rather than for an impression or a click. The ads appear above other results on Google Search and Google Maps for queries like "emergency plumber" and show a business name, star rating, hours, service area and a verification badge. The format exists because Google wanted to sell to small trades that had little appetite for keyword auctions, and because consumers searching for someone to enter their home want some assurance the provider is real, licensed and insured. Verification, not keyword selection, is the price of entry.
How the format works
An advertiser does not choose keywords. It selects service categories (water heater repair, drain cleaning, divorce law) and a service area defined by postcodes, cities or regions. Google matches searches to those categories itself. Before any ad runs, the business must pass screening and verification, which according to Google's help centre takes about three to four weeks after documents are submitted. Depending on the category and country, checks cover business registration, the owner or a business representative, individual field workers, state or provincial licences, liability insurance and, for lawyers, a state bar licence per attorney. A verified Google Business Profile is mandatory for every category.
Google routes each contact through a tracked number or its own messaging and booking tools, and charges when that contact counts as a valid lead. Pricing has shifted over time. At the 2017 relaunch, Google set a fixed price per lead by job type and area, which Kim Spalding, then product director for small and medium business ads, described as "balancing what we know about cost of jobs and overall demand", according to Search Engine Land. Bidding arrived in October 2020, according to agency Blue Corona, with a manual maximum bid per lead and an automated Maximize Leads mode. Target Cost Per Lead was added in September 2024 as a middle option that lets individual leads cost more or less than an average target, with Google stating that the monthly budget would never be exceeded.
Ranking depends on three groups of signals, according to Google's "About ad rankings" page: the bid, which acts as a ceiling; the likelihood of producing a lead, which covers responsiveness, search context, relevance and whether messaging or booking is enabled; and profile quality, meaning rating, review count, average response time, images and completed verification checks. Google adds that higher-quality profiles "may pay lower costs per lead". Since August 2024, Google has selected photos from advertiser profiles automatically for inclusion in some ads.
Google publishes no lead prices. A CallMath calculator cited by PPC Land uses 40 dollars as an example: on 40 calls a month, missed-call billing alone produces about 5.76 charged leads, or 230.40 dollars a month, under its assumptions about answer rates.
Badges, guarantees and disputes
For most of its history the format carried two badges. Google Guaranteed, introduced in late 2016 for home services, came with a money-back promise: Google would refund a dissatisfied customer up to the invoice amount, with a lifetime cap of 2,000 dollars, according to Search Engine Journal. The European version, launched in 2020, capped refunds at 1,500 euros or 1,500 pounds, according to Search Engine Land. Google Screened covered professional services such as lawyers, financial planners and estate agents. It required licence and background checks but offered no refund. A third mark, License Verified by Google, appeared later for some trades.
Google merged all of these into a single Google Verified badge from October 2025, according to Search Engine Land and Search Engine Journal, both reporting in August 2025. Google's help page for the new badge states that the Money Back Guarantee is discontinued: only bookings made before December 7, 2025, remain eligible for reimbursement, within 30 days of the job's completion. Existing verified advertisers received the badge automatically. Google says the badge does not affect ranking.
Disputes followed a similar arc. Advertisers once flagged bad leads manually within 30 days. From July 2024, Google's models began reviewing every lead and crediting invalid ones automatically, according to Search Engine Land, and leads tagged "job type not serviced" or "geo not serviced" stopped qualifying for credit. Ginny Marvin, Google's Ads Liaison, said on X that Google was "proactively evaluating every lead that comes in against an equitable set of standards". Google's current help page excludes health care verticals, tax specialists and advertisers in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) from automatic credits.
Origin and evolution
The product began as Home Services Ads. Moz's Pete Meyers spotted a test on July 29, 2015, showing ads for plumbers and locksmiths in San Francisco, and a Google spokesperson confirmed it was "testing a new experience for local searches in the San Francisco Bay Area", according to Search Engine Land.
On October 31, 2017, Google renamed the programme Local Services by Google, moved management out of AdWords Express into a dedicated app and set a target of 30 US cities by the end of that year, up from 17, according to MediaPost. Professional services followed: a pilot with lawyers, financial planners and estate agents in San Diego and Houston began in August 2019, and a national US launch under the Google Screened label came on July 28, 2020, according to Search Engine Land. Nine European countries received home services the same year, and on September 12, 2023, Google extended the format to legal firms and estate agents in London, according to Google's own blog. As of October 2026, Google's help centre covers the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Belgium and Austria.
The programme has since been drawn steadily closer to the rest of Google's local stack. Booking systems for Business Profiles and Local Services Ads were merged from August 2024, and review management moved to Business Profile on July 11, 2025.
Why it matters
For trades with high-value jobs, the format sits at the top of the results page and charges only on contact, shifting part of the risk of wasted spend away from the business. For agencies it is a separate discipline: with no keywords, ad copy or landing pages, the levers are verification, reviews, call handling and budget. Answer rates are therefore commercial variables. Invoca's July 2026 benchmarks, reported by PPC Land, found that people answer 52% of inbound home-services calls, falling to 34% in HVAC.
The format also matters as a structural signal. Lead marketplaces such as Angi, HomeAdvisor and Thumbtack sell essentially the same product, and Google's version occupies space above them on its own results page. Competition for the category is widening: in September 2026 Amazon began placing Yelp-supplied plumber and roofer ads on order confirmation pages.
Limitations and disputes
Google controls the definition of a lead, and that definition keeps moving. From October 1, 2026, missed calls during business hours that ring for more than 20 seconds became billable leads, as did qualifying follow-up calls. The notice did not say when the 20-second clock starts or how disputes over such calls would work. Google's Ads Liaison later said follow-up calls from the same person within 15 days are charged only once.
Features have also been removed by vertical. In January 2025 tax specialists lost message leads, automatic credits, booking and call recording without an official explanation. Terms dated March 20, 2025 grant Google an "irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free license" over submitted content and the right to crawl supplied URLs, while keeping binding arbitration. Documentation is not fully consistent either: Google's screening page still refers to a "Google Screened" badge for estate agents in some US states after the October 2025 consolidation. Sources also disagree on the 2020 European roll-out, which Google's 2023 blog put at nine countries while Search Engine Land's launch report listed ten, including the Netherlands.
Not the same as
Google Ads search campaigns run on keywords chosen by the advertiser, are priced per click in an auction and send traffic to a landing page; match types govern which queries trigger them. Performance Max is Google's goal-based campaign type across all its inventory, built from headlines, images and videos; Explaining Performance Max covers it. Local Services campaigns now use the Performance Max label but serve only on Search and Maps and ignore those creative assets. Location ads in the local pack, the sponsored pins whose share of tracked mobile keywords rose to about 22% in January 2026, are bought through standard campaigns with location assets; see Explaining local pack. Meta's local and lead ads target people by radius and demographics on Facebook and Instagram and are generally billed on impressions or clicks, with no licence verification; Explaining lead ads covers the form-based variant.
Recent developments
The standalone product is being dismantled. In July 2026 Google said it would move Local Services campaigns into Google Ads as a pay-per-lead Performance Max type. Phase one began in August 2026 for selected US home and storefront advertisers; service-area businesses follow in late 2026 and non-US accounts in 2027. Pay-per-lead billing and keywordless targeting survive. Manual maximum bids, vertical-level targets and Better Business Bureau callouts do not, and historical reports are lost once the dashboard closes, with 14 days' notice to export. Name, address and hours now sync one way from Business Profile, the same record that drives hyperlocal advertising and organic map results. As of October 2026, new pay-per-lead campaigns still cannot be created inside Google Ads.

- October 8, 2020: Bidding introduced, with maximum bid per lead and Maximize Leads

- August 7, 2024: Automated photo selection announced

- September 2024: Target Cost Per Lead bidding launched
- January 6, 2025: Tax specialists lose message leads, autocredits, booking and call recording
- March 20, 2025: New terms grant Google a licence over submitted content
- July 11, 2025: Review management moves to Business Profile

- August 2026: Phase one migration begins for selected US advertisers
- October 1, 2026: Missed calls over 20 seconds become billable leads
- Late 2026: Service-area businesses scheduled to migrate
- 2027: Non-US accounts and remaining categories scheduled to migrate

Summary
Who: Google runs the format and verifies advertisers; buyers are local service businesses such as plumbers, electricians, lawyers, estate agents and cleaners, often managed by specialist agencies.
What: A pay-per-lead ad format that charges for calls, messages and bookings rather than clicks, targets by service category and area rather than keywords, and requires background, licence and insurance checks behind a Google Verified badge.
When: Tested as Home Services Ads in July 2015, renamed in October 2017, expanded to professional services in 2020 and Europe the same year, consolidated under one badge in October 2025 and migrating into Google Ads from August 2026.
Where: Google Search and Google Maps, in the US, Canada and nine European countries as of October 2026.
Why: To sell advertising to small trades that avoid keyword auctions and to give consumers some assurance about providers who enter their homes.
